Bartonella, Rodents, Fleas and Ticks: a Molecular Field Study
on Host-Vector-Pathogen Associations in Saxony,
Eastern Germany
Cornelia Silaghi1,2 & Martin Pfeffer3 & Daniel Kiefer1,4 & Matthias Kiefer5 &
Anna Obiegala3
Received: 11 March 2016 /Accepted: 10 May 2016
Springer Science+Business Media New York 2016
Abstract Bartonellae cause zoonotic diseases and are trans-
mitted by arthropods. Rodents are reservoirs for most
Bartonella spp. As the knowledge about Bartonella in rodents
and their parasitizing ectoparasites is scarce in Germany, this
study’s objectives were to investigate Bartonella spp. in small
mammals and in their ectoparasites. A total of 79 small mam-
mals (seven species) were captured and their ectoparasites
collected at seven sites around Leipzig, Saxony, Germany, in
2010 and 2011. Altogether, 79 spleen samples, 135 fleas (five
species) and 365 ticks (three species) were investigated for
Bartonella spp. by PCR targeting the ITS 16S–23S rRNA
region. In total, 52

small mammals were positive for uncultured Bartonella sp.

. This study’s results suggest that rodents
and fleas may be reservoirs and vectors, respectively.
Zoonotic B. grahamii and B. elizabethae were found in ro-
dents and their fleas. Therefore, humans may contract
Bartonella infection by contact to wild rodents. Ticks seem
of minor importance in transmitting Bartonella spp. found in
fleas and rodents. However, ticks might be vectors of
B. chomelii.
Keywords Apodemus flavicollis . Myodes glareolus .
Ctenophthalmus nobilis . Bartonella spp. . Ixodes ricinus
Introduction
Bartonella spp. are facultative intracellular alpha-
proteobacteria (order Rhizobiales, family Bartonellaceae)
and the causative agents of bartonellosis which may result in
severe clinical symptoms in humans and domesticated ani-
mals worldwide [39]. Bartonellosis, depending on the infect-
ing Bartonella species, may cause chronical (e.g. verruga
peruana) and acute (e.g. cat scratch fever) infections displayed
by a variety of clinical symptoms [26, 40]. Bartonella
quintana, Bartonella bacilliformis and Bartonella henselae
are the most common causative agents and are carried by
humans and cats (B. henselae) respectively [39]. However,
there is an increasing number of clinical reports in humans
caused by other bartonellae such as Bartonella elizabethae
and Bartonella grahamii which are harboured by rodents
[53]. While varying prevalences of bartonellae were found
in wild ungulates, carnivores and domesticated animals [9,
12, 19, 32], the highest prevalence and diversity of
Bartonella spp. were reported in rodents which are considered
to be main reservoirs. To date, about 30 Bartonella species are

latter are known to be of zoonotic potential (B. grahamii,
B. elizabethae, Bartonella vinsonii subsp. arupensis,
Bartonella washoensis and Bartonella tamiae) [14]. High
prevalences of Bartonella spp. were reported in rodents from
Asian [51]
), African [29]
and American coun-
tries [22]
. In Europe, the prevalence of Bartonella spp.
in rodents is ranging from 13.7 to
in studies from
Poland [35, 54], Slovenia [21], Spain [13], France [8] and
the UK [49].
Bartonella spp. are mainly transmitted by haematophagous
arthropod vectors such as fleas, lice, sandflies and ticks [2, 4,
14, 44]. Other vectors such as the woodlouse hunter spider
(Dysdera crocata) have been suggested as vectors as well
[27]. Amongst ectoparasites infesting rodents, fleas are ex-
pected to be main vectors for Bartonella spp. [3, 52].
Ctenophthalmus nobilis also known as Ctenophthalmus
agyrtes, the most common flea species parasitizing rodents
in Central Europe, is known to transmit B. grahamii and
B. taylorii to Myodes glareolus [5]. In European countries
such as Poland [38], Italy [42], the Netherlands [44] and
France [15], Bartonella spp. were detected in Ixodes ricinus,
the most common tick in Central Europe [41]. However, data
on Bartonella species in rodents and their parasitizing ecto-
parasites, such as C. nobilis and I. ricinus, is lacking in
Germany and information about host-vector-pathogen associ-
ations of the latter are scarce in Europe. Thus, this study’s
objectives were to analyse (1) the occurrence of Bartonella
species in rodents, their fleas and ticks and (2) to identify their
host-vector-pathogen associations in Germany.
Materials and Methods
Study Sites
The study site was divided in five animal trapping areas
located around the city centre of Leipzig in Saxony which
were formerly consecutively named from E to I [45]. Sites
E–G are part of the BLeipziger Neuseenland^ (http://www.
leipzigerneuseenland.de/), a recultivated former brown
coal mining area which is surrounding a lake (Lake
Cospuden, 436 ha) and which belongs to the largest
recreational area near Leipzig. Site H is a recreational
city park called BPark Lößnig-Dölitz^ (http://www.
leipzig.de/de/buerger/freizeit/leipzig/parks/park_loessnig/)
, near Leipzig which contains several ponds. This park
merges into forested areas and is located near a
renatured waste disposal mountain. Site I (42 ha) is a
game park, located in Leipzig, often frequented by visi-
tors, which belongs to one of the largest riparian forests in
Germany (www.leipziger-auwald.de). About 250 game
animals are present (http://www.leipzig.de/de/buerger/
freizeit/leipzig/parks/wildpark/wissen/). The study site
and trapping areas have been described in detail in
previous studies [45].
Sampling of Small Mammals
Small mammals were trapped with Sherman
live animal
traps (H. B. Sherman Traps, Inc., Tallahassee, FL, USA) in
2010 and 2011 (official trapping permit: 36.11-36.45.12/4/10-
026-MH, 364.60/2009-102-2). Traps, baited with apple slices,
were placed for at least two consecutive nights per month and
site and were checked twice a day. Small mammals were cap-
tured with at least 20 traps per subdivided area per month in
August and October in 2010, from March to June in 2011
(sites E, H, I) and further in November 2011. Collected ani-
mals were anaesthetized with
\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }
, euthanized by cervical
dislocation and then stored at
- 8 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }
until further examina-
tions in the laboratory. Details about small mammal trapping
were published before [30]. All small mammals were morpho-
logically identified [48]. Bycaught small mammal species,
found dead in traps or brought by a cat, were additionally
verified by the use of a conventional PCR targeting the partial
cytochrome
b
gene (354 bp) as described previously [34, 45].
Necropsy was carried out and spleens from the small mam-
mals were collected.
Collection of Ticks and Fleas
Ectoparasites were collected from the trapped small mammals
with tweezers and stored separately for each small mammal in
1.5-ml-sized tubes at
- 8 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }
(Eppendorf, Hamburg,
Germany) until further examination. The morphological iden-
tification of fleas and ticks was performed under a stereomi-
croscope with standardised taxonomic keys [17, 36, 37, 47].
Fleas and ticks were kept individually in separate 2.0-ml-sized
tubes (Eppendorf) for the following DNA extraction.
DNA Extraction
DNA samples of spleens
) and ticks
) from the
small mammals were available from a previous study on tick-
borne infectious agents [45]. DNA extraction from collected
fleas was carried out for each flea individually with the
QIAamp DNA Mini Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) as previ-
ously described [46]. Quantity and quality of the extracted
DNA were determined with a spectrophotometer (Nano
Drop ND-1000, Erlangen, Germany).
Polymerase Chain Reaction
A conventional PCR targeting 635 bp of the 16S–23S ITS
region was performed for detection of Bartonella spp. as
C. Silaghi et al.
Springer
described [25, 43], followed by UV light analysis on
agarose gel dyed with GelRed (Biotium, Hayward CA, USA).
Sequence Analysis
PCR products were purified with the QIAquick PCR product
purification Kit (Qiagen) according to the manufacturer’s in-
structions and sequenced commercially by Eurofins MWG
Operon (Martinsried, Germany). Sequences were analysed
with Chromas Lite® (Technelysium Pty Ltd., South
Brisbane, Australia) and compared with sequences obtained
from GenBank using BLASTn (National Center for
Biotechnology Information, Bethesda MD, USA) as previous-
ly described [43]. Analysed and aligned sequences were de-
posited in GenBank under the following Acc. Nos.:
Statistical Analysis
Confidence intervals
( 9 5 \ \% \mathrm { C I } )
for prevalences of
Bartonella spp. in small mammals, ticks and fleas were
determined by the Clopper and Pearson method with
GraphPad Software (GraphPad Software Inc., San
Diego, CA, USA). Independence of compared small sam-
ple sizes
was tested with Fisher’s exact test. The
Kruskal-Wallis test with a Bonferroni correction and a
significance level of
was used to test the inde-
pendence of flea infestation on rodents per study site. The
t test was used to test the independence of flea infestation
on M. glareolus and Apodemus spp.

Host-Vector-Pathogen Associations
The complexity of relations between Bartonella spp., flea and
rodent species is shown in Fig. 1. In both fleas and in rodents,
uncultured Bartonella spp. were most commonly detected.
The figures shows clearly that Bartonella spp. detected in most
flea and rodent species are very diverse and that there is just a
single host-vector-pathogen association between
M. glareolus, Me. turbidus and B. grahamii.
Discussion
In comparison to other mammals, the highest diversity of
Bartonella spp. was described in rodents to date. Altogether,
22 rodent-associated Bartonella spp. and subspecies were de-

to other animals and humans [31].
T. europaea and Ar. terrestris were, though not infested
with fleas, positive for Bartonella spp. in our study. It is prob-
able that those small mammals, which were found dead due to
being caught by a cat, were not infested with fleas due to the
survival strategy of fleas which jump off dead hosts as soon as
the hosts’ body temperature is decreasing [18]. The high in-
festation rate of fleas on small mammals at site BI^ could be
due to the high density of captured rodents and may explain
why the majority of Bartonella-positive rodents were found
there. Fleas vary greatly in their degree of host specificity,
from being highly host-specific to host-opportunistic [24].
Most flea species showed a preference for certain rodent spe-
cies in our study. As Me. turbidus was found predominantly
on

. glareolus and C. nobilis and N. fasciatus significantly
more often on Apodemus spp., it seems likely that these flea
species have a host preference, but no clear host specificity.
In our study, the prevalences for Bartonella spp. were high
in most rodent flea species such as C. nobilis
N. fasciatus
and Me. turbidus
). There are
only few studies investigating those flea species for the occur-
rence of Bartonella spp. However, B. taylorii and B. grahamii
are known to be transmitted by C. nobilis to M. glareolus [5].
Bartonella sp. has previously been described in N. fasciatus
[33]. The prevalence of Bartonella spp. in fleas seemed to be
independent of the Bartonella species and of the prevalence in
their rodent hosts as most positive fleas derived either from
negative rodents or from rodents which were not positive for
the same Bartonella species. This observation has been made
before, with the conclusion of a vertical transmission path for
Bartonella in fleas [7]. B. grahamii, B. taylorii and
B. elizabethae are known to occur in fleas which infest rodents
[53]. In our study, these Bartonella spp. as well as several
uncultured Bartonella spp. were found in fleas. Though
B. elizabethae is known to occur in rodents and fleas, we
detected this Bartonella species exclusively in fleas [6].
B. grahamii was more abundant in Me. turbidus fleas com-
pared to other flea species. In accordance with this finding,
B. grahamii was mainly found in M. glareolus, the main host
of Me. turbidus, suggesting a host-vector-pathogen associa-
tion for M. glareolus, Me. turbidus and B. grahamii. Apart
from this observation, no other significant host-vector-
pathogen associations were found.
To date, it is not clear whether ticks are involved in the
natural life cycle of Bartonella spp. Their epidemiological
importance has been considered secondary [16, 28, 50].
However, previous studies from Italy, France, Portugal and
Germany reported prevalences ranging between 1.5 and
in questing I. ricinus ticks respectively in I. ricinus
removed from humans [10, 15, 20, 42]. In our study, the prev-
alence is in the range of the mentioned European studies
). The Bartonella species detected in ticks in this study
were B. chomelii, B. grahamii, B. taylorii and uncultured
Bartonella sp. The prevalence in I. ricinus was significantly
higher when compared to
D
. reticulatus. Thus, D. reticulatus
appears to be less important in the transmission cycle of
Bartonella spp. than I. ricinus. Comparing the results for
Bartonella in ticks and fleas, ticks seem to be more dependent
on the prevalence and Bartonella sp. detected in their rodent
hosts in contrast to fleas. Most positive ticks were collected
from positive rodents in our study, and the Bartonella sp.
found in ticks were mainly matching the species found in their
rodent hosts. These results suggest that ticks, reflecting the
infection in their rodent hosts, are of minor importance in
the natural life cycle of Bartonella spp. found in rodents and
their fleas. However, B. chomelii was exclusively found in
ticks but not in fleas and rodent hosts from this study.
Formerly, B. chomelii was detected in domesticated ruminants
and in their engorged ticks from Spain and Italy [1, 11]. Cattle
are suggested to be reservoirs not showing any clinical symp-
toms [1]. As B. chomelii has never been detected in fleas and
rodents thus far, this Bartonella sp. is likely to be transmitted
transovarially in tick populations in nature as most positive
ticks deriving from rodents were larvae which were naïve
before feeding on their rodent hosts.
Conclusion
In conclusion, a high prevalence of different Bartonella
species was found in rodents and their fleas with a high
diversity and a tendency towards a host-vector-pathogen
association for M. glareolus, Me. turbidus and
B. grahamii. Zoonotic bartonellae such as B. grahamii
and B. elizabethae were found in rodents and their fleas
in this study. Therefore, humans and their companion
animals are at risk of contracting Bartonella infection
by direct or indirect contact to infected blood of wild
living rodents. Ticks seem to be of minor importance in
the transmission cycle of Bartonella sp. found in fleas
and rodents. However, ticks may play an important role
as vectors in the transmission of B. chomelii.
